title: Compact Action Widgets & Unified SDK Playbook (PRD draft)
summary: Introduce an SDK-first protocol for small, structured 'action widgets' embedded in incremental streaming responses. Goal is to provide a low-latency, developer-friendly surface for tool invocation, UI widgets, and typed partial-results while preserving graceful degradation and low client complexity.
goals: Define a compact framing format for embedding executable/interactive units (action widgets) into streaming responses
Standardize a minimal handshake for tool-calls inside streams that supports idempotency, partial-apply, and rollbacks
Provide a unified SDK surface (JS + Python) with two ergonomic primitives: StreamReader (incremental) and WidgetClient (declarative tool binding)
Keep end-to-end median token latency increase < 5ms for typical chat workloads compared to current streaming baseline
Provide clear migration guides for existing streaming SDK users and examples for common use-cases (chat buttons, form-fill, code-runner, search snippets)
non_goals: Not building a full RPC surface—this is specifically for lightweight action attachments in streaming output
No attempts to replace asynchronous long-running job orchestration (those remain via Dedicated/Private patterns)
We will not ship a mobile-native SDK in phase-1 (focus on web/node/python desktop SDK ergonomics)
Not mandating a single UI rendering for widgets—clients may render action widgets however they like
success_metrics: Adoption: 25% of new hosted-api streaming integrations use WidgetClient within 3 months of launch
Performance: median incremental token emission latency < previous baseline + 5ms on 95th perc model mix
Reliability: tool-call success rate >= 99.5% under normal load (no fallthrough to full response required)
Developer feedback: average SDK satisfaction score >= 4.2/5 from beta cohort
risks_and_mitigation: Semantic drift: widgets become overly complex -> mitigation: limit widget schema to max 6 fields and require explicit versioning
Backpressure complexity on clients -> mitigation: SDK exposes simple backpressure APIs and default buffering heuristics
Tool safety and replay hazards -> mitigation: idempotency tokens + server-side tool call audit logs and optional manual confirmation step
Observability gaps -> mitigation: emit standardized telemetry events (widget-emitted, widget-invoked, widget-rolledback) to Console
proposed_api_surface:
Two primary SDK primitives explained in README-style prose:

- StreamReader: subscribe to incremental events (text delta, widget frames, checkpoints). Provides simple async iterator (python) / async generator (js) and a small event handler to receive 'widget' frames.
- WidgetClient: declarative binding of widget types to local handlers. Handles idempotency tokens, optimistic UI state, and automatic retries. SDK performs serialization, exponential backoff on tool-call failures, and transparent fallback to full-text continuation if the widget call cannot be resolved.

Server API: streaming responses include interleaved frames: TEXT_DELTA | WIDGET_FRAME | CHECKPOINT. Widget frames are compact jsonl blobs with explicit schema-version header (v1). Example frame: {"v":"1","id":"w-3f2","type":"search_snippet","payload":{...},"commit_hint":"optimistic"}.
streaming_handshake_details:
Handshake flow (simplified):
1) Client opens streaming call with ?features=widgets and capability hints (max_widget_size, prefer_sync_tool_calls).
2) Server responds with STREAM_START frame listing supported widget types and max payload size.
3) On WIDGET_FRAME, SDK emits an opaque Widget object to application handler. Handler can call widget.invoke(params) -> returns a promise/future.
4) Widget.invoke issues a short non-blocking post to the Workspace tool endpoint via the same session token; server processes, responds with a WIDGET_RESULT frame which is then applied as a delta.

Key constraints: widget lifecycle ties to stream session id; server may garbage-collect pending widgets after session TTL. For safety, tool-invokes include idempotency_key and explicit 'commit_hint' to indicate whether the action should be persisted or treated as ephemeral.
sdk_ergonomics_notes:
Principles: small surface area, explicit is better than magic, default-safe behaviors.

JS ergonomics:
- Async iterator for text deltas: for await (const chunk of StreamReader(...)) { if (chunk.type==='widget') widgetClient.bind(chunk) }
- WidgetClient.bind returns a lightweight Widget with .render() and .invoke() helpers. Default render: JSON preview + action button; customers can override.

Python ergonomics:
- Async generator + helper context manager: async with StreamReader(...) as s: async for ev in s: handle(ev)
- WidgetClient exposes sync wrapper that will offload to threadpool for simple sync code patterns.

Backpressure model: SDK exposes two knobs: max_inflight_widgets (default 8) and max_buffered_deltas. When max_inflight_widgets exceeded, clients can choose drop-latest (cheap) or block-new (backpressure). Default is drop-latest with user-visible telemetry event.
observability_and_operations:
Telemetry events to emit (Console + Tracing): widget.emitted, widget.bound, widget.invoked, widget.result.received, widget.rollback, widget.timeout. Each event should include model_name, route, session_id, widget_id, duration_ms, and error_code (if any).

SRE runbook: widget invocation timeouts default 2.5s; on increased timeouts fallbacks to full-text generation with an explicit 'fallback_reason' logged. For canary environments, enable widget-invoke sampling at 100% to observe behavior.
migration_plan:
Phase 0 (alpha): SDKs (js/python) with opt-in flag; docs + samples (todo list below).
Phase 1 (beta): default enable for new streaming routes, provide migration guide for existing customers and CLI tool to annotate old client integrations.
Phase 2 (GA): enable across routes with metrics dashboard, deprecation notices for legacy untyped widget frames.

Customer-facing migration notes: provide a 'no-op' widget render that degrades to text if client does not understand widgets. Encourage partners to adopt WidgetClient for robust behavior.
open_questions: Should widget frames be limited by bytes or by number of fields? (tradeoff: developer expressivity vs perf)
Is a single universal widget type (with a 'schema' field) better than multiple typed widgets from a compatibility standpoint?
How do we handle cross-session widget handoffs (e.g., user leaves page then returns)? Keep-orphaned-state?
Do we allow widget-invoke to call external customer webhooks directly, or must all tool calls go via Redwood-hosted tool proxies?

content:
Notes to reviewers:

This is intentionally pragmatic — the aim is to give SDK-first teams a low-friction way to surface small interactive attachments inside streams without forcing them into a heavyweight RPC model. The widget idea is intentionally narrow: small, versioned, and render-agnostic.

Design rationale (short): developers want the ability to present a compact actionable item (search result with 'open' button, code snippet with 'run' action, calendar suggestion with 'add' button) that is emitted as part of a streaming reply. The current heavy pattern (client receives a tokenized text suggestion -> makes separate API call to run tool) adds round trips and UX flakiness. Embedding a compact action widget reduces round trips and gives the server a standardized way to express intent.

Edge-case thoughts: widget storms (model emits many small widgets) — SDK default limits, plus server-side rate-limiting with a 'widget_rate' hint in the STREAM_START response. We should also consider an admin toggle per-tenant to disable widgets.

Please comment on the schema-size limit and the safety model for tool-invokes. If you want to play with a quick prototype, fork the sample repo linked above and try the demo: simple chat that emits a 'search_snippet' widget when the model detects a factual query.

Slack thread: #product-hosted-api (pinned links to early sketches). Jira epic: RID-3421.

End of draft.
